note: These are v0 evals. They exist to make the skill testable and to invite community contributions. Each case describes a realistic scenario and the shape of output that a good application of the skill should produce. PRs adding cases, sharpening assertions, or reporting cases where the skill fails are welcome.

evals.name: decide-whether-to-sprint
evals.prompt: We're a B2B SaaS startup (20 people, post-PMF, ~$2M ARR). We've been debating for 3 months whether to redesign our onboarding flow or add a new reporting feature. The CEO and Head of Product disagree on the direction. Should we run a sprint?
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) identify this as a strong Sprint candidate — high stakes, team stuck, Decider available (CEO); (b) recommend Sprint as the tool because the question is testable with a prototype and 5 customers; (c) help the user formulate Sprint Questions that would resolve the debate ('Will new users complete onboarding without help?' or 'Will existing users adopt the reporting feature?'); (d) name the CEO as the Decider and explain what that means; (e) note that they might need two separate sprints (one for onboarding, one for reporting) rather than trying to sprint on both at once; (f) NOT just say 'yes, run a sprint' without checking the prerequisites.
assertions: Output identifies the situation as a strong Sprint candidate (high stakes, stuck, Decider available)
Output helps formulate specific, testable Sprint Questions
Output names the CEO as the likely Decider and explains the Decider role
Output suggests focusing on ONE question per sprint, not both
Output checks prerequisites (team availability, customer access for Friday)
Output cites Knapp or the Sprint book at least once

evals.name: plan-monday-exercises
evals.prompt: It's Monday morning of our sprint. We're an e-commerce startup testing whether a personalized shopping experience (AI-driven recommendations) will increase conversion. Our Decider is the VP of Product. Walk me through today.
evals.expected_output: Output should walk through Monday's exercises in order: (a) set a long-term goal ('become the go-to personalized shopping platform'); (b) write Sprint Questions that are specific and testable ('Will customers trust AI recommendations?' 'Will personalization increase add-to-cart rate?'); (c) draw the Map — customer journey from landing page to checkout; (d) Ask the Experts — suggest inviting customer support lead, data analyst, someone from the AI team; (e) How Might We notes during expert talks; (f) organize and dot-vote on HMW notes; (g) the Decider (VP of Product) picks the target — one customer type, one moment on the Map. Output should insist on the Note-and-Vote pattern for decisions and NOT skip any exercise.
assertions: Output walks through all Monday exercises in order (goal, Sprint Questions, Map, experts, HMW, vote, target)
Output helps write specific, testable Sprint Questions (not vague)
Output describes the Map exercise concretely
Output suggests specific expert types to invite
Output explains How Might We note-taking
Output has the Decider (VP of Product) pick the target, not the group consensus
Output mentions Note-and-Vote or silent voting

evals.name: push-back-on-group-brainstorming
evals.prompt: We're on Tuesday of our sprint. My team lead suggested we do a brainstorming session this afternoon instead of the individual sketching exercises. She says brainstorming is more collaborative and will produce better ideas. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Output should push back firmly but kindly on the brainstorming suggestion. Specifically it should: (a) cite Knapp's anti-brainstorming stance and the research behind it (Charlan Nemeth); (b) explain why individual work produces better ideas — avoids anchoring, prevents deference to seniority, forces everyone to think independently; (c) describe the actual Tuesday exercises (Lightning Demos, Notes, Ideas, Crazy 8s, Solution Sketch) and why they're sequenced this way; (d) explain that the sketches will be evaluated together on Wednesday through a structured process (Art Museum, Heat Map, Speed Critique) — collaboration happens through evaluation, not ideation; (e) NOT compromise by saying 'maybe brainstorm first, then sketch.'
assertions: Output pushes back on group brainstorming, does not accept the suggestion
Output cites Knapp's anti-brainstorming stance or Nemeth's research
Output explains why individual work produces better ideas (anchoring, deference, independent thinking)
Output describes the actual Tuesday exercises as the alternative
Output explains that collaboration happens through Wednesday's evaluation, not Tuesday's ideation
Output does NOT compromise by blending brainstorming with sketching

evals.name: prototype-strategy-for-non-tech-product
evals.prompt: It's Thursday of our sprint. We're a healthcare startup and our prototype needs to show a patient intake process — a form that asks medical history questions, then shows a personalized care plan. Our team is mostly clinical people, not designers. How do we build this prototype in one day?
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) recommend Keynote/Google Slides or Figma as the prototype tool — not code, not a real form; (b) explain Goldilocks quality — the prototype needs to look real enough that patients react honestly, but it's a facade; (c) assign prototype team roles (Maker, Stitcher, Writer, Asset Collector, Interviewer); (d) emphasize the Writer role especially for a healthcare product — medical language matters; (e) suggest using real-looking but fake medical data; (f) recommend a trial run at 3-4 PM; (g) remind them the prototype is disposable — it will be thrown away after Friday; (h) NOT suggest building a real form or connecting to a real database.
assertions: Output recommends Keynote/Slides/Figma over code for the prototype
Output explains Goldilocks quality (real enough to test, rough enough to discard)
Output assigns prototype team roles (Maker, Stitcher, Writer, Asset Collector, Interviewer)
Output emphasizes the Writer role for medical/clinical language
Output recommends a trial run Thursday afternoon
Output explicitly says the prototype is a facade, not a real product
Output does NOT suggest building real functionality

evals.name: sprint-vs-shape-up-comparison
evals.prompt: My team is trying to decide between running a Sprint (Jake Knapp) and adopting Shape Up (Ryan Singer). We're a post-PMF B2B SaaS with 30 people. We need to figure out a major new feature direction AND we need a sustainable development methodology. What should we use?
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) identify that Sprint and Shape Up solve different problems — Sprint is a one-time 5-day intervention to answer a big question; Shape Up is an ongoing development methodology for shipping features; (b) recommend Sprint for the 'figure out the feature direction' question — run a sprint to test the concept with customers; (c) recommend Shape Up for the 'sustainable development methodology' need — 6-week cycles, shaping, betting, building; (d) explain how they compose — Sprint first to validate the direction, then Shape Up to ship it; (e) NOT recommend one over the other as a blanket answer; (f) cite both Knapp and Singer.
assertions: Output identifies Sprint and Shape Up as solving different problems (intervention vs. methodology)
Output recommends Sprint for the feature direction question
Output recommends Shape Up for the ongoing methodology need
Output explains how Sprint and Shape Up compose (Sprint first, then Shape Up)
Output does NOT recommend one as universally better than the other
Output cites both Knapp and Singer (or their respective books)
